Design and Religion: Indelible Experiences

May 6, 2026 · Van Sedita · 3 min read

We envision a world where design and religion work together to spread love, empathy, and charity faster than divisiveness, selfishness, and hate. To achieve this, we aim to bring the stories of those driving this change, both big and small, into the spotlight, allowing ideas for positive transformation to spread quickly and reach those who need them most.

That is the heart/mission/reason for the podcast.

We want to bring the stories of people driving positive change, both big and small, into the spotlight so those ideas can move quickly, reach the people who need them most, and leave a lasting mark.

For me, the show is a way to explore two industries in flux.And yes, I see religion as an industry.

Some data places it around $1.2 trillion. To put that in perspective, that is nearly six times the size of the professional design services market.

When we talk about Design and Religion, we are talking about two of the most powerful systems we have for shaping how billions of people spend their time, money, attention, and energy.

Both create experiences people carry with them.

Can you identify with:

A beautifully designed service made you feel seen?
A harmful system that made you feel invisible.
A ritual that offered comfort for decades when repeated?

A careless institution can leave a wound that lasts just as long. That is what I mean by indelible experiences.

They are the moments that mark us. They teach us whether we belong. They teach us whether we are safe. They teach us whether we matter. They teach us whether help will arrive when we need it.

On the surface, design and religion can seem like separate worlds: one concerned with the material, the other with the eternal. But both work through human experience. Both shape memory, trust, behavior, and meaning.

Both ask deeply human questions:

How do we find true belonging? How do communities care for one another in crisis? How do institutions build trust? How do we repair what has caused harm?

What I’ve learned through this journey is that religion is as much an experience as it is a belief system. The way a person is welcomed, heard, supported, judged, or excluded leaves a lasting mark.

Design works the same way. Every system we build teaches the people using it something about how we, the builders, value them.

I am drawn in deeply by the exploration of the human systems we inherit, the ones we question, and the ones we have a responsibility to redesign with more intentional care.

We started the show to explore that connection in a world that, lately, seems to enjoy breaking connections.
